The Goldblotch grouper Epinephelus diacanthus is a demersal serranid that attains a maximum recorded total length of 55 centimeters [Li = 55 centimeters], a size that places it among the medium-bodied members of its genus across the Indo-Pacific. Newly fertilised eggs, which are pelagic and undergo rapid cleavage-stage development, have an average diameter of 0.8 millimeters, a figure that was used to derive the estimated wet weight at birth of approximately 0.000268 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000268 grams] for the yolk-sac larva upon eclosion. This minute starting mass reflects the typical energy-poor yolk reserves of broadcast-spawning serranids, where thousands of small, buoyant eggs are released into the water column during a single spawning event. The species is iteroparous and exhibits a relatively fast initial growth trajectory during the pelagic larval phase, with individuals transitioning to the benthic juvenile stage after several weeks of feeding on copepod nauplii and other microzooplankton. Field surveys along the western coast of India indicate that post-settlement juveniles recruit to rocky reef habitats at sizes well below 10 centimeters total length, where they remain closely associated with crevices and overhangs during the first year of life.

Reproductive maturation in Epinephelus diacanthus is reached at a total length of 39.2 centimeters [Lp = 39.2 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds to the onset of gonadal recrudescence in both sexes. Individuals of this size exhibit clear histological evidence of vitellogenesis in females and active spermatogenesis in males, indicating that puberty is attained well before the species achieves its asymptotic body dimensions. The corresponding wet weight at puberty has been estimated from length-weight regressions at approximately 737 grams [Wwp = approximately 737 grams], a body mass that allows the fish to allocate substantial resources toward the development of mature gametes. This length and weight at maturity are consistent with values reported for other medium-bodied groupers in the Epinephelus genus, where a total length equivalent to roughly seventy percent of the ultimate length marks the transition to reproductive viability. Field studies conducted in the Gulf of Mannar have shown that females first become reproductively active at around four years of age, though the exact timing can vary with local food availability and temperature regimes typical of tropical reef ecosystems.

The maximum reproductive output of the Goldblotch grouper has been evaluated under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable water temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. Under these conditions, the maximum daily egg production rate reaches approximately 68 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 68 eggs per day], a value that reflects the species capacity for sustained batch spawning over an extended breeding season. This species is a batch spawner, releasing multiple clutches over the course of several months, with individual spawning events producing an estimated 4,000 to 5,000 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 4,000 to 5,000 eggs per clutch] and the frequency of spawning events reaching approximately 5 to 6 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 5 to 6 clutches per year]. The maximum daily egg production rate thus reflects both the high fecundity per spawning event and the temporal compression of reproductive activity into the warmest months of the year. At the same temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], researchers have also documented the maximum lifespan of this species, with the oldest individuals recorded in mark-recapture studies surviving for 21 years [am = 21 years]. This longevity is typical of many slow-growing, late-maturing serranids and underscores the life-history trade-off between extended somatic persistence and high annual fecundity.

The maximum adult wet weight attained by Epinephelus diacanthus has been calculated from the length-weight relationship specific to this species, yielding an asymptotic body mass of 2000 grams [Wwi = 2000 grams] for individuals that reach the ultimate total length of 55 centimeters. This allometric relationship, derived from a large sample of commercially landed fish across the species range, shows a curvilinear increase in mass with length that is characteristic of groupers and other robust-bodied reef fishes. The adult body mass of two kilograms places the Goldblotch grouper at an intermediate trophic position within its community, where it feeds predominantly on crustaceans and small teleosts. In comparison, the hatchling wet weight of 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams] represents a mass amplification factor of over seven million from the yolk-sac larva to the fully grown adult, a remarkable ontogenetic trajectory that is achieved through a combination of rapid early growth and sustained, moderate feeding throughout the juvenile and adult stages. This massive size increase also has implications for the species vulnerability to fishing pressure, as late-maturing individuals are particularly susceptible to stock depletion before they have had the opportunity to reproduce.

Comparative analyses of life-history traits across the Serranidae indicate that the Goldblotch grouper exhibits a reproductive schedule that is intermediate between the short-lived, highly fecund coral trout species and the long-lived, low-fecundity giant groupers. The total length at puberty of 39.2 centimeters [Lp = 39.2 centimeters] represents approximately seventy-one percent of the ultimate length, a proportion that is consistent with the general pattern among tropical groupers where maturity is delayed until a substantial fraction of asymptotic size is reached. Similarly, the wet weight at puberty of 737 grams [Wwp = 737 grams] corresponds to roughly thirty-seven percent of the ultimate wet weight of 2000 grams [Wwi = 2000 grams], a ratio that reflects the positive allometric scaling of mass with length in this species. Under a thermal regime of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the maximum lifespan of 21 years [am = 21 years] facilitates multiple reproductive seasons, allowing iteroparous females to offset the high early mortality typical of pelagic eggs and larvae. The daily egg production rate, when integrated over the spawning season, provides a per-capita reproductive output that is sufficient to maintain populations under moderate exploitation, though stocks remain vulnerable to overfishing given the delayed maturation and relatively low natural mortality of adults.
